nodes.statement:
Therefore, $B^i_{k,\ell'}(c,d) \leq B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d)$ for all
        $i\neq k$. 
        We conclude that 2) holds.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity in the job index

nodes.name: Assume tau_{k,l} unfinished at d
nodes.statement: We use an indirect proof strategy and assume that $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is not finished by time $d$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume tau_{k,l} unfinished at d

nodes.name: tau_k active throughout [c,d)
nodes.statement:
In this case, $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is active during $[r_{k,\ell},d)$.
		Since $r_{k,\ell}\leq c$ or $\tau_k$ is active during $[c,r_{k,\ell})$, we conclude that $\tau_k$ is also active during $[c,d)$.
nodes.statement_short: tau_k active throughout [c,d)

nodes.name: Lemma 15 contradicts the hypothesis
nodes.statement:
Lemma~\ref{lem:non-sched} states that Equation~\eqref{eq:prop:backbone_prep} does not hold.
		This contradicts our assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 15 contradicts the hypothesis

nodes.name: Instantiate Proposition 16 with d
nodes.statement:
This corollary follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:backbone_prep} by setting $d:=r_{k,\ell} + \widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$.
		The case $c>d$ does not occur since otherwise $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \geq  c-r_{k,\ell} > \widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ would hold by definition of $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ and $d$.
		We only consider $c \leq d$.
nodes.statement_short: Instantiate Proposition 16 with d

nodes.name: Bound the B terms by those over [c,d_{k,l})
nodes.statement:
Since $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \leq D_k$ by assumption, we have $d\leq d_{k,\ell}$.
		Hence, $B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d)\leq B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell})$ and $B_{k,j}(c,d) \leq B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell})$ for all $i$ and all $j$.
		As a result, the left hand side of Equation~\eqref{eq:prop:backbone_prep} is less than or equal to $(C_k+ S_k) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell})$, which is the same as $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} + r_{k,\ell} - c = d-c$ by definition.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the B terms by those over [c,d_{k,l})

nodes.name: Conclude response-time bound
nodes.statement:
Since all assumptions from Proposition~\ref{prop:backbone_prep} hold, the job $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is finished by time $d=\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} + r_{k,\ell}$.
		Hence, $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude response-time bound

nodes.name: Release window of relevant jobs
nodes.statement:
A job of $\tau_i$ can only be executed during $[c,d_{k,\ell})$, if it is released after $c-\widetilde{R}_i$.
		Moreover, it can have higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$, if it is released no later than $r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k - \Pi_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Release window of relevant jobs

nodes.name: Count releases in the window
nodes.statement:
We count the maximal number of releases of $\tau_i$ during $(c-\widetilde{R}_i, r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k - \Pi_i)$ by $\ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k - \Pi_i - c + \widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}}$ if the interval has non-negative length.
		Otherwise, the number of releases is $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Count releases in the window

nodes.name: No interfering job: bound trivial
nodes.statement: If there is no job of $\tau_i$ executed during $[c,d_{k,\ell})$, then $B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell})=0$ and the lemma is proven.
nodes.statement_short: No interfering job: bound trivial

nodes.name: Otherwise isolate the last interfering job
nodes.statement:
Otherwise, let $\tau_{i,j'}$ be the last job of $\tau_i$ being executed during $[c,d_{k,\ell})$.
		We isolate that job in the following way.
		Let $r_{i,j'}$ be the release time of $\tau_{i,j'}$ and let $C^*$ be the amount of time that the processor is working on $\tau_{i,j'}$ during the interval $[c,d_{k,\ell})$.
		We have $B(c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq B(c,r_{i,j'}) + C^*.$



		
		If $r_{i,j'}-c < (C-C^*)$, then $B(c,r_{i,j'}) + C^* \leq C$.
		Moreover, $\ceiling{\frac{D_k-C_i+r_{k,\ell}-c+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}}C_i \geq \ceiling{\frac{D_k+r_{k,\ell}-c}{T_i}}C_i \geq C_i$ since there is a job being executed during $[c, d_{k,\ell})$, i.e., $c < D_k+r_{k,\ell}$.
		In this case the lemma is proven.
		
		If $r_{i,j'}-c \geq (C-C^*)$, then $B(c,r_{i,j'}) + C^* \leq B(c + (C_i-C^*),r_{i,j'}) + C_i$, i.e., we over approximate be replacing $(C_i-C^*)$ time units at the beginning by execution time.
		Next we compute $B(c + (C_i-C^*),r_{i,j'})$ by counting the number of releases during the interval $(c+(C_i-C^*)-\widetilde{R}_i, r_{i,j'}-T_i]$.
		It is 

		$
			\ceiling{\frac{r_{i,j'}-T_i-c-C_i+C*+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}} 
			\leq \ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell}-T_i-c-C_i+D_k+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}}
			= \ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell}-c-C_i+D_k+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}} -1
		$

		where we use that $r_{i,j'} + C^* \leq r_{k,\ell} + D_k$.
		In total, the value of $B(c,d_{k,\ell})$ is then upper bounded by $\ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell}-c-C_i+D_k+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}} \cdot C_i$ in this case.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise isolate the last interfering job

nodes.name: Set up induction over jobs ordered by priority
nodes.statement:
Assume we have found $b_k,~k=1,\dots,n$ such that Equation~\eqref{eq:suff_sched_test_fixed} holds.
		We consider some schedule obtained by this task set and denote by $Seq$ the sequence of all jobs in the schedule ordered by their priority.
		Via induction, we prove that the first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ have the required response time upper bound, for all $\xi \in \Nbb_0$.
		Consequently, $\widetilde{R}_k$ is an upper bound on the worst-case response time of $\tau_k$ for all $k$ and the task set is schedulable.
nodes.statement_short: Set up induction over jobs ordered by priority

nodes.name: Base case: empty set
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Initial case:} $\xi = 0$.
		In this case, the set of the first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ is $\{\}$ the empty set.
		Trivially, all of them have the required response time upper bound.
nodes.statement_short: Base case: empty set

nodes.name: Inductive step via Analysis Backbone
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Induction step:} $\xi \to \xi+1$.
		By assumption, the first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ have the required response time upper bound.
		We denote the $(\xi+1)$-th job in $Seq$ by $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
		We aim to use Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone} to prove that the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is upper bounded by $\widetilde{R}_k$.
		
		By definition, we have $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} = (C_k+ S_k) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + c - r_{k,\ell}$.
		Since all higher priority jobs have the required response time upper bound, we can use the estimation from Section~\ref{sec:estimation_B}.
		Using Lemma~\ref{lem:upper_bound_sum_Bkj} and Lemma~\ref{lem:total_bound_interference}, we obtain $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \leq \widetilde{R}_k$ when choosing $c:= b_k+r_{k,\ell}$.
		Due to Equation~\eqref{eq:suff_sched_test_fixed}, even
		$\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \leq \widetilde{R}_k \leq D_k$.



		We use Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone} to conclude that $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ and therefore $\widetilde{R}_k$ is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step via Analysis Backbone

nodes.name: Choice of c satisfies the backbone restriction
nodes.statement:
Since $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a+1)$-th job in an active interval, $\tau_k$ is active during $[r_{k,\ell-a}, r_{k,\ell})$.
		Hence, the restriction on $c$ in Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone} are fulfilled by default, when $c$ is chosen from $[r_{k,\ell-a}, d_{k,\ell})$.
nodes.statement_short: Choice of c satisfies the backbone restriction

nodes.name: Self-interference at most a(C_k+S_k)
nodes.statement:
Moreover, since $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a+1)$-th job in an active interval, the jobs $\tau_{k,1}, \dots, \tau_{k,\ell-a-1}$ are finished by time $r_{k,\ell-a}$.
		We obtain $\sum_{j < \ell-a} B_{k,j} (c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq \sum_{j < \ell-a} B_{k,j} (r_{k,\ell-a},d_{k,\ell}) = 0$.
		Hence, 

		$
			\sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j} (c,d_{k,\ell}) 
			= \sum_{j = \ell-a}^{\ell-1} B_{k,j} (c,d_{k,\ell})
			\leq \sum_{j = \ell-a}^{\ell-1} (C_k+S_k)
			= a\cdot (C_k+S_k).

		$
nodes.statement_short: Self-interference at most a(C_k+S_k)

nodes.name: Combine with Bound B2 and conclude
nodes.statement:
We combine this with the results from Lemma~\ref{lem:upper_bound_sum_Bkj} and Lemma~\ref{lem:total_bound_interference}, and obtain that $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ from Equation~\eqref{eq:cor_sched_test} is less than or equal to the value in Equation~\eqref{eq:lem_var_window}.
		If \eqref{eq:lem_var_window} is at most $D_k$, then $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}\leq D_k$.
		Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone} states that $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ is an upper bound on the response time of $r_{k,\ell}$ and therefore, also \eqref{eq:lem_var_window} is an upper bound on the response time.
nodes.statement_short: Combine with Bound B2 and conclude

nodes.name: Induction plan with two bounds
nodes.statement:
The proof is similar to the one of Theorem~\ref{thm:suff_sched_test_fixed}.
		Let $Seq$ be the sequence of all jobs in the schedule ordered by their priority.
		By induction we show that the following response time upper bound holds for the first $\xi \in \Nbb_0$ jobs in $Seq$:

nodes.statement_short: Bound 1: R_k for all jobs

nodes.name: Bound 2: T_k for tilde-a-th jobs
nodes.statement: $T_k$ for all $\tilde a_k$-th jobs in an active interval of $\tau_k$ for each task $\tau_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound 2: T_k for tilde-a-th jobs

nodes.name: Base case trivial
nodes.statement: \textbf{Initial case:} $\xi_0$. The initial case is again trivially fulfilled, since there has nothing to be checked when there are no jobs.
nodes.statement_short: Base case trivial

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Induction step:} $\xi \to \xi+1$.
		The first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ have the required response time upper bounds 1) and 2) by induction.
		We denote by $\tau_{k,\ell}$ the $(\xi+1)$-th job of $Seq$.
		Let $a$ be the lowest value in $\Nbb_0$, such that $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a+1)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$.
		We first show that $a\leq \tilde a_k$ by contraposition.
		If $a > \tilde a$, then we consider the job $\tau_{k,\ell-(a-\tilde a)}$.
		This is the $(\tilde a+1)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$.
		Moreover, this job is one of the first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ and therefore has a response time of at most $T_k$ due to 2).
		Hence, $\tau_{k,\ell-(a-\tilde a)}$ is finished by time $r_{k,\ell-(a-\tilde a)+1}$.
		We conclude that $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a-\tilde a_k)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$, which contradicts the minimality of $a$.
		We now choose $c:=b^a_k-a\cdot T_k + r_{k,\ell}$.
		Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:suff_sched_test_var_prep} with this $c$ shows that $\widetilde{R}^a_k(b^a_k)$ is a response time upper bound of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ as required.

nodes.name: Reason 1: bounded active intervals required
nodes.statement:
First, the analysis with variable analysis window can only analyze schedules where the length of active intervals is bounded.
More specifically, if the response-time upper bound $\widetilde{R}^a_k$ is in the interval $(T_k, D_k)$ for all $a$, then the schedulability test with the variable analysis window never deems the task schedulable.
nodes.section: 4.5 Dominance of Fixed and Variable Analysis Window
nodes.statement_short: Reason 1: bounded active intervals required

nodes.name: Reason 2: max_a intensifies the effect
nodes.statement:
Second, by setting $max\_a$ this effect is even intensified:
The analysis with variable analysis window has to find $\widetilde{R}^a_k \leq T_k$ even for some $a \leq max\_a$.
nodes.section: 4.5 Dominance of Fixed and Variable Analysis Window
nodes.statement_short: Reason 2: max_a intensifies the effect

nodes.name: Reason 3: discretization checks different points
nodes.statement:
Third, the discretization using $\eta$ in Algorithm~\ref{alg:sched_test_fixed} and~\ref{alg:sched_test_var} ensures the same number of points for each analysis interval.
As a result, not all points $b+aT_k$ with $b$ from Algorithm~\ref{alg:sched_test_fixed} are checked during Algorithm~\ref{alg:sched_test_var} as well.
nodes.section: 4.5 Dominance of Fixed and Variable Analysis Window
nodes.statement_short: Reason 3: discretization checks different points

nodes.name: On arrival, select and run the highest-priority job
nodes.statement: when a job is added to the ready queue, the new highest-priority job is determined and executed.
nodes.statement_short: On arrival, select and run the highest-priority job

nodes.name: On finish or suspension, remove job and reselect
nodes.statement: Whenever a job finishes or suspends itself, it is removed from the ready queue and a new highest-priority job has to be determined and is executed.
nodes.statement_short: On finish or suspension, remove job and reselect

nodes.name: Map job priority to its absolute deadline at release
nodes.statement: At each job release, its priority should be identified with its absolute deadline, and necessary priority mapping operations should be performed.
nodes.statement_short: Map job priority to its absolute deadline at release

nodes.name: Insert job into priority-ordered ready queue
nodes.statement: The job context is placed into the ready queue according to its priority, which is commonly realized by a dedicated data structure, e.g., a red-black tree in RTEMS and a binomial heap in {$\text{LITMUS}^{\text{RT}}$}.
nodes.statement_short: Insert job into priority-ordered ready queue

nodes.name: Run a highest-priority job, resolving ties
nodes.statement: One highest priority job should be executed. In case there are deadline ties, a regulation should be performed. This step also takes place if a job finishes its execution.
nodes.statement_short: Run a highest-priority job, resolving ties

nodes.name: 500 task sets per utilization level, 50 tasks each
nodes.statement:
For the experiments, we synthesize $500$ task sets for each utilization from $0\%$ to $100\%$ in steps of $5\%$.
	For each task set we generate $50$ tasks.
nodes.statement_short: 500 task sets per utilization level, 50 tasks each

nodes.name: Draw utilizations with UUniFast and periods log-uniformly
nodes.statement: We first generate $50$ utilization values $U_i$ using the UUniFast~\cite{DBLP:journals/rts/BiniB05} method with the given total utilization goal, and then adopt the suggestion by Emberson~et~al.~\cite{emberson2010techniques} to pull the minimum inter-arrival time $T_i$ according to a log-uniform distribution from the interval $[1,100] [ms]$.
nodes.statement_short: Draw utilizations with UUniFast and periods log-uniformly

nodes.name: Set WCET from utilization and implicit deadlines
nodes.statement: The worst-case execution time is computed by $C_i = T_i \cdot U_i$ and the deadline is set to the minimum inter-arrival time $D_i = T_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Set WCET from utilization and implicit deadlines

nodes.name: Draw suspension times uniformly
nodes.statement: For each task, we draw the maximum suspension time $S_i$ uniformly at random from $[0,0.5(T_i-C_i)]$.
nodes.statement_short: Draw suspension times uniformly
